notes.meaning: Jesus chose a larger group of disciples beyond the twelve apostles and sent them out in pairs. They went ahead as heralds to prepare each town and village He planned to visit. Traveling two by two gave them companions for encouragement and provided two witnesses to confirm their message.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern critical scholars questioned whether this mission happened, suggesting it was simply an imitation of the earlier sending of the twelve apostles.

notes.meaning: Jesus told His disciples that many people were ready to turn to God, like a ripe field waiting for harvest. However, there were not nearly enough workers to gather them all. He commanded them to pray that God, the true owner of the harvest, would urgently call and send out more workers into the world.

Jesus sent His followers into the world knowing they would face harsh opposition and mistreatment from an unfriendly culture. Like innocent and defenseless lambs surrounded by wolves, they were not to use violence or force. Instead, they had to rely completely on the care and protection of the Good Shepherd.

The disciples were told to travel light, without money bags, extra travel sacks, or spare sandals, trusting God to supply their daily needs through others. They were also told not to stop for long greetings on the road. Eastern greetings involved lengthy social rituals, and their mission was too urgent for delay.

Whenever the disciples entered a home, their first words were to be a spoken blessing of peace on the household. This greeting was more than polite manners; it offered God's spiritual wholeness, blessing, and goodwill to the family. It showed that the gospel arrives as a message of peace rather than condemnation.

If someone living in the house was open and ready to welcome God's message, the offered peace would rest on that home. But if the people rejected them, the blessing would not be lost; it would return to the messenger. God's gift of peace is never wasted, even when people turn it away.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The phrase means that God's salvation has entered the home of anyone who willingly welcomes Christ's messengers.

notes.meaning: The messengers were to stay in that first welcoming home and eat whatever was provided, rather than moving around to look for better food or lodging. Jesus explained that spiritual workers earn their support, so receiving meals was fair pay for their labors rather than mere charity. Accepting basic hospitality frees ministers to focus on their work.

When a town welcomed the disciples, they were to accept and eat whatever meal their hosts put before them. They were not to complain about plain food or worry about strict religious food traditions. Being gracious guests kept their attention on the urgent proclamation of God's grace.

Jesus told them to heal the sick in the town as a compassionate and visible proof of God's power. Along with healing bodies, they were to announce that the kingdom of God—His royal, saving presence—had come right to them. Miracles served as real signs that the Messiah's rule was active and close at hand.

If a town refused to welcome the disciples, they were to go into its public streets and deliver a solemn warning. By publicly wiping the town's dust from their feet, they showed that they broke fellowship with those who rejected Christ. Even so, they still had to announce that God's kingdom had arrived at their doorstep.

Jesus warned that on the final judgment day, the notoriously wicked city of Sodom would face a lighter penalty than a town rejecting the gospel. Sodom was deeply corrupt, but it had never received the direct presence and message of Christ. Rejecting greater spiritual light brings far greater guilt and accountability.

Jesus spoke sorrowful words of judgment against Chorazin and Bethsaida, towns near the Sea of Galilee that had witnessed many of His miracles. He declared that if ancient pagan cities like Tyre and Sidon had seen the same wonders, they would have repented long ago in deep sorrow. Having great spiritual privileges without turning from sin brings terrible ruin.

Because of their refusal to believe, Chorazin and Bethsaida will face a heavier sentence at the judgment than the pagan cities of Tyre and Sidon. God holds people accountable according to the truth and evidence they were given. Greater opportunities to see God's work make stubborn unbelief far more serious.

Capernaum had served as Jesus' ministry headquarters, enjoying extraordinary blessings and miracles as if lifted up to heaven itself. Yet because its people remained proud and unrepentant, Jesus warned that the town would be cast down to Hades, the realm of death and ruin. Outward spiritual privileges cannot rescue anyone whose heart remains unchanged.

Jesus assured His messengers that they acted as His official ambassadors. Anyone who listened to their preaching was truly listening to Christ, and anyone who rejected them was rejecting Him and the Father who sent Him. Believers can take comfort knowing that the world's response to the gospel is really directed at God Himself.

The disciples came back from their mission overflowing with excitement and joy. They were astonished that even evil spirits obeyed their commands when they used the name and authority of Jesus. Their joy came from discovering firsthand that Christ's power worked through them against the forces of darkness.

Jesus told them that while they were out ministering, He saw Satan falling from heaven as quickly and visibly as lightning. The disciples' victories over demons signaled the sudden collapse of the devil's tyrannical rule. Through the preaching of the gospel, Satan's power is decisively overthrown.

Jesus confirmed that He had given His followers authority over the enemy's harmful power, pictured as trampling on dangerous snakes and scorpions. God promised to protect His servants from spiritual ruin as they carried out His work. This assurance offers real comfort of God's keeping power, though it is never an excuse to take foolish chances.

Jesus warned His disciples not to make spiritual power or authority over demons their chief source of joy. Miraculous gifts and power are only temporary, but salvation lasts forever. Their greatest happiness should be that God has registered their names as citizens of heaven in His book of life.

In that moment, Jesus was filled with deep joy through the Holy Spirit and praised the Father as Lord of all creation. He gave thanks that God kept His saving truth from the proudly wise of this world and revealed it to humble, childlike people. God's plan delights in lifting up the lowly and hiding pride from human hearts.

differ.view: God in His sovereign grace chooses according to His own good pleasure to withhold saving truth from the worldly-wise and reveal it to the elect.
God does not arbitrarily hide salvation, but allows the proudly self-sufficient to remain blind while freely pouring out grace on the humble.
